Q: What does "SbkConverter::copyToPython is null" mean? A:

tl;dr

PySide uses Shiboken to convert Qt (C++) types into Python objects.

Fix1: Workaround

Perhaps, the converters didn't get registered before import of the wrapper. Try this:

from PySide6.QtWebEngineCore import QWebEngineExtensionInfo  # force-load wrapper
exts = ext_man.extensions()
print(exts)

If this returns None (or not what you are expecting) it's a real missing-binding issue/bug.

Fix2: You possibly encountered a PySide bug: report it! You can do this here

This is a huge help for the community!

One more fix attempt (Upgrade)

Try to upgrade PySide6 / Qt for Python (if you can)

  • Because this API is new (Qt 6.10+), the most likely real fix is upgrading to the newest PySide6 build available for your Python/Constraints/etc.
  • If you're on Linux and installed via distro packages, consider using the official PyPI wheels instead.
  • (almost) The same as messing/mixing numpy/cython core, mixing Qt/PySide pieces from different sources can produce erratic behaviour.

Details

When you call:

ext_man.extensions()
  • Qt is effectively returning something like a QList<QWebEngineExtensionInfo>.
  • PySide then tries to convert each QWebEngineExtensionInfo element to a Python wrapper object.

This is the key part you gave, in the warning msg:

SbkConverter::copyToPython is null for "PySide6.QtWebEngineCore.QWebEngineExtensionInfo"

  • Meaning: PySide does not have a "copy-to-Python" converter registered for that type.
  • Then, it can't create/materialize the Cpp objects as Python objects.
  • I believe this hits a 'fallback result': The list you saw: [None, None] (placeholders where the wrappers should have been).
  • Why do you think so?: Beause if I was implementing I would fallback like that.

Docs do not seem to be correct/complete (bug theory)

  • According to Qt's docs, QWebEngineExtensionManager.extensions() is "supposed to provide a list of QWebEngineExtensionInfo" (verbatum).
  • extensionManager() / QWebEngineExtensionManager are new in Qt 6.10.
  • That's why I think this might be a incomplete/buggy Python binding, for your particular return type / version.

If you decide to report as bug

I will conveniently repost the bug report page (no, I am not a Qt 'developer/collaborator').

And ask you to include specifically:

  • PySide6 version: Do python -c "import PySide6 as ps; print(ps.__version__)
  • Qt version: PySide6.QtCore.qVersion()
  • platform (it's important; just Linux <Distro> or Windows or Darwin [MacOS]) + Python version (do: python --version)
  • minimal repro (basically what you pasted; but there you can paste full, except sensitive parts if any)

Small diagnostic script

You can also send to them with the print results (if you report bug).

import PySide6
from PySide6.QtCore import qVersion
from PySide6.QtWebEngineCore import QWebEngineProfile
from platform import python_version

print("Python:", python_version())
print("PySide6:", PySide6.__version__)
print("Qt:", qVersion())

PySide6.QtWidgets.QApplication()
p = QWebEngineProfile("test")
m = p.extensionManager()
print("manager:", m)
print("extensions():", m.extensions())

Q: Is it possible to provide manually-calculated percentages to tqdm? A:

If you are willing to round your percentages to an integer value, then:

import time

from tqdm import tqdm

with tqdm(total=100.0) as bar:
    last_percentage = 0
    for percentage in (7.3, 22.8, 44.9, 77.2, 91.6, 100.0):
        time.sleep(1)
        new_percentage = round(percentage, 0)
        increment_percentage = new_percentage - last_percentage
        last_percentage = new_percentage
        bar.update(increment_percentage)

Q: Generate random numbers between two limits and fixed value in vba A:

maxValue is 108. 20 * 108 = 2160 so if all your values end up being 108 in the first 19 cells (improbable, but certainly possible), then your last cell will have to be 2100 - 19 * 108 = 2100 - 2052 = 48, which would be bad.

If all your values end up being 100 in the first 19 cells, another improbable, but possible scenario, then your last cell will be 2100 - 1900 = 200. Again, unacceptable.

The solution is to always adjust the minimal and maximum value of your randomization to ensure that your value are still acceptable. If your total needs to be 2100, then its 5% = 105, so if all your cells are 105, then their sum is correct. Hence, it would make sense to say that maxValue is ~= total / (20 - i + 1) + diff and minValue is ~= total / (20 - i + 1) - diff. Of course, in each step, total will be smaller than before and i incremented This way the randomized value will stay close to the average of the current total at each step. Try this approach, maybe it's already good-enough, but if not, then you can adjust it. If you need to keep it always between 100 and 110, for example and you randomized some values so far, then after each randomization see whether the other cells could still be in the interval you expect and if your current random would force the other cells to move out from the threshold somewhere, then repeat the randomization of your current cell.

Q: How to use TailwindCSS with Vite? (not react or something just vanilla JS) A:

TailwindCSS v4 - Understanding the changes compared to v3

With the release of Tailwind CSS v4, several breaking changes occurred:

There is no longer a need for tailwind.config.js. Consequently, running npx tailwindcss init during installation - which used to create this file - is no longer necessary. Instead, only CSS-first configuration should be used.

There is no longer a need for the @tailwind directive; instead, a single central import must be known and used.

With the new CSS-based configuration, many things have changed. It's now possible to declare functional utilities, manage namespaces, introduce new variants, or override existing ones.

Due to these breaking changes, the following update is straightforward to follow, and introducing multiple packages also makes sense.

Since the init process is no longer needed, there's no reason to include the Tailwind CLI in the main package by default. For this reason, the original package has been split into three parts:

  • tailwindcss - contains only the interpreter required for CSS imports
  • @tailwindcss/cli - provides the Tailwind CLI without the init process
  • @tailwindcss/postcss - provides the PostCSS plugin

Therefore, using Tailwind CSS in any way requires installing tailwindcss itself plus at least one of the other plugins.

Since Tailwind CSS relies on Lightning CSS under the hood, it makes sense to drop PostCSS wherever possible. For this reason, another plugin has been released:

  • @tailwindcss/vite - provides a Vite plugin that allows using Tailwind CSS without PostCSS

TailwindCSS v4 via Vite - Installation steps in light of the changes

Although Vite supports PostCSS, Tailwind no longer really needs it and relies on Lightning CSS instead, so using the Vite plugin reduces the project overhead.

npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite

vite.config.ts

import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    tailwindcss(),
  ],
});

References:

  • What's breaking changes from v4?
  • TailwindCSS v4: Upgrade guide by rozsazoltan
  • TailwindCSS v4: more packages and new Vite support

Vite 8 compatibility

I don't want to duplicate the installation steps, as they will change after the stable release of Vite 8. Therefore, I recommend following the reference below in the Vite 8 beta until the full installation steps are updated.

Rolldown-Vite (expected to become the default from Vite 8) replaces the previous Vite engine. It relies on Rust instead of JS; and Lightning CSS (Rust based) instead of esbuild (JS based).

However, Rolldown-Vite applies Lightning CSS to the CSS output even during development. Clear, correct support between Tailwind CSS v4 and Rolldown does not yet exist. It is necessary for the Vite Lightning CSS configuration to be aware of the Lightning CSS settings preferred by Tailwind CSS; otherwise, it may produce incorrect or unexpected results.

vite.config.ts

import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    cssMinify: 'esbuild', // default: 'lightningcss'
  },
  plugins: [
    tailwindcss(),
  ],
});

References:

  • Installing the TailwindCSS Vite plugin with Vite 8 - peer vite@"^5.2.0 || ^6 || ^7" from @tailwindcss/vite@4.1
  • tailwindlabs/tailwindcss discussion #19624
  • https://vite.dev/guide/features#lightning-css
  • OKLCH colors are converted to LAB colors when I start using Rolldown-Vite instead of Vite
